name: solar-system

description.en: 52 cards on stable facts about the Solar System: the eight planets in order from the Sun, the five dwarf planets the IAU recognises and where they orbit, the largest moon of each planet that has moons, which planet (or, for Charon, dwarf planet) 16 well-known moons orbit, and undisputed superlatives such as the largest, hottest and densest planet. Front: a question or description, e.g. "4th planet from the Sun"; back: the planet, moon or place in English and Swedish, with a note where it helps. Facts from NASA Science and Wikidata, checked against JPL's Solar System Dynamics tables, the IAU and the Swedish Wikipedia.
description.sv: 52 kort med beständiga fakta om solsystemet: de åtta planeterna i ordning från solen, de fem dvärgplaneter som IAU erkänner och var de kretsar, den största månen hos varje planet som har månar, vilken planet (för Charon dvärgplanet) 16 välkända månar kretsar kring och obestridda fakta om vilken planet som är störst, hetast, tätast och så vidare. Framsida: en fråga eller beskrivning, t.ex. ”Fjärde planeten från solen”; baksida: planeten, månen eller platsen på engelska och svenska, med en anteckning där den hjälper. Uppgifterna kommer från NASA Science och Wikidata och är kontrollerade mot JPL:s tabeller (Solar System Dynamics), IAU och den svenskspråkiga Wikipedia.

method: Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.

Scope: the editor's brief asked for about 50 cards of stable, unambiguous Solar System facts: the planets in order, the IAU's dwarf planets and where they orbit, the largest moon of each planet that has moons, notable moons and their planets, and undisputed superlatives, avoiding moon counts, varying distances and anything recently revised.

NASA pages: the script fetch_nasa.py (query 6) downloaded 37 pages of NASA Science (science.nasa.gov) and the NASA media usage guidelines, saved the HTML and a plain-text rendering, and the texts were searched for the sentences each card needed (planet order, "largest", "smallest", "hottest", "densest", "least dense", "shortest day", "sideways", "retrograde", "largest moon", "only moon", "volcanically active", "Kuiper Belt", "asteroid belt"; query 7 and the moon-page search, query 8). NASA's Planets page and Dwarf Planets page fetched today still list eight planets and "five officially recognized dwarf planets", which is the recency check for the dwarf planets (a 2025 candidate such as 2017 OF201 is not recognised by the IAU).

Wikidata: a first label-based query (query 1) timed out (HTTP 504). Query 2 listed the natural satellites of Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune and Pluto (items with P397 parent astronomical body, at least 40 sitelinks) with English and Swedish labels; query 3 the labels and classes of the Sun and planets; query 4 the items that are instances of dwarf planet (Q2199), which include non-IAU bodies such as Sedna and lack Makemake as a truthy value; Makemake's item (Q604) was found with the search API (query 5). The script entities.py (query 9) fetched the labels and aliases in English, Swedish and mul, and the statements P31, P361, P397, P2054, P2120, P2146, P2147, P2386 and others, for all the items; search.py (query 10) found the items of the Kuiper Belt, the asteroid belt, the Great Red Spot and the scattered disc.

Selection of the cards from the brief: the eight planets in order (fronts "1st planet from the Sun" … / "Första planeten från solen" …); the five dwarf planets the IAU recognises, each with where it orbits, plus Ceres as the only dwarf planet in the inner Solar System; the largest moon of each of the six planets with moons (Mercury and Venus have none); the parent of 16 well-known moons (the four Galilean moons, Titan, Enceladus, Mimas, Iapetus, Triton, Phobos, Deimos, Titania, Oberon, Miranda, Ariel, and Charon of the dwarf planet Pluto); and 16 superlatives and features that NASA states outright and that JPL's tables, Wikidata or the Swedish Wikipedia confirm.

Cross-check against JPL: the Planetary Physical Parameters and Planetary Satellite Physical Parameters pages (query 11) were saved and read: the planets' sidereal orbital periods increase in the order of the cards, Jupiter has the largest and Mercury the smallest mean radius, Earth the highest (5.5134 g/cm³) and Saturn the lowest (0.6871) bulk density, Jupiter the shortest (0.41354 d) and Venus the longest (−243.018 d) sidereal rotation; the dwarf-planet table lists exactly Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Makemake and Haumea; the satellite table gives each moon under its planet and confirms the largest moon of each planet (Phobos 11.08 km > Deimos 6.2 km; Titania 788.9 km > Oberon 761.4 km; Ganymede 2631.20 km, the largest of all, then Titan 2574.76 km).

Cross-check against the IAU: the current www.iau.org no longer serves the public theme pages (HTTP 404), so the archived pages on iauarchive.eso.org were fetched (query 12): "Naming of Astronomical Objects" lists the five dwarf planets and says all but Ceres orbit beyond Neptune; "Pluto and the Developing Landscape of Our Solar System" says New Horizons showed Pluto's diameter to be larger than Eris's.

Swedish text: the Swedish names are the Wikidata Swedish labels (Merkurius, jorden, Saturnus, Neptunus, månen, Ganymedes, Japetus, Stora röda fläcken, Kuiperbältet …). The script svwiki.py (query 13) took each item's Swedish Wikipedia sitelink and fetched the article's introduction and current revision id through the MediaWiki API; every card's Swedish name was found in the introduction, which is quoted, with its revision, in the evidence. The Swedish names jorden and månen are written in lower case, as the Wikidata labels and Swedish usage have them; the Swedish Museum of Natural History's fact cards for schools (query 14) were read as a check of that usage ("Jorden är den tredje planeten från solen."). Card fronts and notes are the compiler's own Swedish. The Swedish term "den spridda skivan" in the note of dwarf-planet-eris is the compiler's translation of "scattered disc": Wikidata has no Swedish label for it (Q180380's sv label is the English "Scattered disc"), and the term is used in the Swedish Wikipedia's Pluto article (revision 59725969: "Objekt i den spridda skivan, en dynamiskt instabil region som överlappar Kuiperbältet …"); the note gives the Swedish term alone, without an English gloss (since quality-control round 6).

Wording: every front, back and note is the compiler's own wording of facts from the sources; no sentence is copied. The evidence quotes are short quotations of what each source says, given only so the verification can be repeated. The script make_dossier.py checks that every NASA, Swedish Wikipedia, IAU and museum quote occurs verbatim (whitespace normalised) in the text saved from the source today, and stops if one does not.

Helper scripts (kept in the compiler's working directory, not published; what each does): fetch_nasa.py GETs each URL with the User-Agent above, saves the HTML, removes script/style/noscript elements, turns

, , , , and
into line breaks, strips the other tags, unescapes HTML entities and collapses runs of spaces to save a .txt rendering; sparql.py POSTs a query file to https://query.wikidata.org/sparql (retrying on HTTP 429) and saves the JSON results; entities.py calls wbgetentities (query 9) and prints the labels, aliases and the listed statements; search.py calls wbsearchentities and then wbgetentities for each term (query 10); grep_moons.py applies the pattern in query 8 to the saved NASA moon pages; svwiki.py resolves each item's svwiki sitelink and calls the MediaWiki API with prop=extracts|revisions, exintro=1, explaintext=1 (query 13); make_dossier.py writes this dossier and, before writing, asserts for every NASA, IAU, museum and Swedish Wikipedia quote that the quote with all runs of whitespace replaced by one space is a substring of the saved source text normalised the same way. Evidence added in quality-control round 1 and later was checked against the sources fetched in that round (queries 17–20) in the same way, by hand and with grep.

Machine checks: for every card the builder checks against live Wikidata the English and Swedish labels of the answer and of the bodies named on the front, the parent body (P397) of every moon and planet, and where Wikidata has it a value behind the fact (P31 dwarf planet for Ceres, Pluto, Haumea and Eris, P361 scattered disc of Eris, P2054 Earth's density, P2147 the rotation periods of Jupiter and Venus, P2146 Triton's negative orbital period, P2076 the temperatures of Venus (464 °C mean) and Mercury (700 K maximum) behind hottest-planet, the English alias "Red Planet" of Mars). Checks were skipped, and the reason recorded in quality control, where Wikidata disagrees with better sources or has no label equal to the card's text. The deck was then validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (scripts/validate_sources.ts).

Excluded: after checking, a card on the largest dwarf planet (the sources disagree on Pluto versus Eris, see quality control); by design, without further research, any number of moons, ring or distance figure (changing or varying), the coldest planet (the answer depends on whether the lowest recorded or the mean temperature is meant) and the largest volcano (a superlative not all sources make in the same terms); and, after checking, the planet with the longest day, which is ambiguous (Venus has the longest rotation, Mercury the longest solar day, 176 Earth days, NASA Mercury facts) — the card asks instead which planet takes longest to rotate once on its axis.
selection: Stable facts about the Solar System as of 4 October 2026: the eight planets in order from the Sun; the five dwarf planets recognised by the IAU (Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, Eris) and where each orbits, plus Ceres as the only dwarf planet in the inner Solar System; the largest moon of each of the six planets that have moons (Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune); the planet (or for Charon the dwarf planet) of 16 well-known moons; and 16 superlatives and features that NASA states and an independent source confirms. Left out: moon counts, distances, temperatures as numbers on the front and other values that change with new discoveries or vary by definition; superlatives on which sources disagree (largest dwarf planet, coldest planet, largest volcano) or that are ambiguous (longest day); candidate dwarf planets the IAU has not recognised (Sedna, Quaoar, Gonggong, Orcus, 2017 OF201); and lesser moons. Where an answer has a caveat (Eris's location, Venus's rotation, the Swedish spelling Japetus/Iapetus) a back note states it.

rounds.scope: All 52 cards, the sources and the deck metadata.
rounds.summary: NASA, JPL, the IAU and Wikidata agree on every fact in the cards; where Wikidata disagrees with NASA and JPL (Saturn's density) or lacks a truthy value or a matching label (Makemake's class, the numbered English labels of Haumea and Makemake, the title-case Swedish label of the asteroid belt), the card follows the better sources and the check is not made. Two planned cards were changed or dropped because sources disagree or the question was ambiguous (largest dwarf planet; longest day), and Eris's back was made neutral. Every quote in the evidence was checked by script against the text saved today. The builder's checks cover the labels on every card, every moon's parent body and the Wikidata values behind six of the superlatives. [Correction from quality-control round 3: the claim that NASA, JPL, the IAU and Wikidata agree on every fact overstated the evidence. JPL and the IAU do not address the hottest planet, Io's volcanism, the Great Red Spot or surface water, and at this round the second sources of hottest-planet and most-volcanic-body did not state the fact; both were given real second sources in round 3. The order of the planets was checked against JPL's table of sidereal orbital periods, not by Wikidata checks. Since round 3 the value checks also cover hottest-planet (P2076 of Venus and Mercury).]

findings.issue: NASA's Eris page says Eris is a member of the Kuiper Belt group of objects and also that its orbit "extends far beyond the Kuiper Belt"; Wikidata's P361 for Eris is the scattered disc (Q180380), described as outside the Kuiper Belt; the Swedish Wikipedia calls it a dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt. "Kuiper Belt" on the back would be disputed.
findings.resolution: Back "Beyond Neptune", on which all sources agree (the IAU: all but Ceres orbit beyond Neptune); the back note gives both classifications. Checks: P31 dwarf planet and P361 scattered disc (which the note mentions).

findings.issue: A "largest dwarf planet" card (Pluto) was planned. The IAU's Pluto page says New Horizons showed Pluto's diameter to be larger than Eris's, but JPL's dwarf-planet table gives Eris a mean radius of 1200 km against Pluto's 1188.3 km, NASA's Eris page gives "about 1,500 miles (2,400 kilometers)" against Pluto's 2,377 km and calls Eris "about the same size as Pluto", and the Swedish Wikipedia says Eris has the larger mass.
findings.resolution: Card left out: the sources disagree.

findings.issue: The planned "planet with the longest day" is ambiguous: Venus has the longest rotation (243 Earth days) but Mercury the longest solar day (176 Earth days, NASA Mercury facts; Venus's sunrise to sunset is 117 Earth days).
findings.resolution: Card slowest-rotation asks for the planet that takes longest to rotate once on its axis (Venus; JPL sidereal rotation −243.018 d, Wikidata P2147 −5832.5 h).

findings.issue: Wikidata's P2054 (density) for Saturn has the values 0.867 g/cm³ and 0.19 (unit Q844211), both wrong against JPL's 0.6871 g/cm³ and NASA's statement that Saturn is the least dense planet.
findings.resolution: The card follows NASA and JPL; no Wikidata density check for Saturn (the label checks remain); the discrepancy is in the card's evidence.

findings.issue: Makemake's P31 dwarf planet (Q2199) is at normal rank beside two preferred values (plutoid, cubewano), so it is not a truthy value and a P31 check would fail; the English labels of Makemake and Haumea carry their numbers ("136472 Makemake", "(136108) Haumea") and have no alias equal to the plain name.
findings.resolution: No P31 check for Makemake and no English label check for Makemake or Haumea; their Swedish labels ("Makemake", "Haumea") are checked and NASA, JPL and the IAU confirm both as dwarf planets.

findings.issue: The brief suggested "Jorden" and "Månen" with capitals. The Wikidata Swedish labels are "jorden" and "månen", the Swedish Wikipedia writes them in lower case in running text, and the Swedish Museum of Natural History's fact cards write "jorden", "månen" and "solen" in lower case beside capitalised planet names.
findings.resolution: The Swedish backs are "jorden" (planet-third, densest-planet, liquid-water-surface, largest-rocky-planet) and "månen" (earth-moon), in lower case as Swedish usage and the Wikidata labels have them; capital letters only where a sentence begins.

findings.issue: The Swedish label is "Japetus"; the Swedish Wikipedia says both spellings, Japetus and Iapetus, occur in Swedish texts.
findings.resolution: Swedish front "Japetus" (the Wikidata label and article title); a back note mentions both spellings.

findings.issue: The asteroid belt's Swedish label is capitalised as a title ("Asteroidbältet"), while the back uses it in running text ("I asteroidbältet").
findings.resolution: Only the English label of Q2179 is checked; the Swedish form was checked against the Swedish Wikipedia's running text ("i asteroidbältet", Ceres introduction).

findings.issue: NASA writes that Uranus rotates "at a nearly 90-degree angle from the plane of its orbit" and that its tilt is 97.77 degrees; the Swedish Wikipedia gives 98 degrees. Both describe the same geometry (an obliquity of about 98° puts the axis about 8° from the orbital plane). Wikidata has no obliquity value (its P2045 is the orbital inclination).
findings.resolution: Back note "tilted about 98°, almost in the plane of its orbit"; no Wikidata check of the tilt.

findings.issue: Moon counts differ between sources and change with new discoveries (the museum's fact cards, for example, give Saturn 274 known moons).
findings.resolution: No card or note gives a number of moons, except that Mars has two moons (Phobos and Deimos, stable since 1877; NASA, JPL, the Swedish Wikipedia).

findings.issue: The back note said the storm had been observed for hundreds of years (sv "i flera hundra år"); a 2024 Geophysical Research Letters study finds the present spot is not Cassini's "Permanent Spot" (1665–1713) and has been seen only since 1831.
findings.resolution: Verified: the AGU press release (fetched today) says the spot "has persisted for at least 190 years" and that a clear oval was not seen again "until 1831"; NASA's Jupiter page still says "hundreds of years" and "more than 300 years", and the Swedish Wikipedia says "minst 196 och kanske så mycket som 361 år". Because the age is contested, the note now states no age: "A giant storm larger than Earth." / "En jättestorm, större än jorden." The AGU release was added as a verification source and evidence; the Swedish Wikipedia evidence now quotes its size and age sentences; the NASA evidence notes the conflict.

findings.issue: "In the Kuiper Belt, beyond Neptune" could be read as "always farther out than Neptune", though Pluto was closer to the Sun than Neptune in 1979–1999.
findings.resolution: Verified in NASA's Pluto facts and the Swedish Wikipedia's Pluto introduction (rev 59725969).
